newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: Paraguay torture victims want U.S. compensation. [CORRECTED 07:15 GMT 19/4]
newsitem.headline: Paraguay torture victims want U.S. compensation. [CORRECTED 07:15 GMT 19/4]

text.p: A group of former prisoners of Paraguayan dictator Alfredo Stroessner, toppled in 1989, said on Friday they want compensation from the United States for teaching Stroessner's police torture techniques.

"Officials sent by the United States trained local forces of repression how to torture and martyrize thousands of prisoners of conscience, for which that state should assume responsibility," said former detainee Nemecio Barreto.

About a thousand Paraguayans "disappeared" -- presumed abducted and killed by security forces -- and countless more were detained and tortured during Stroessner's long 1954-1989 dictatorship, according to human rights groups.

Barreto, in an interview with Reuters, accused the U.S. government of giving political support to Stroessner's regime, and named three U.S. officials allegedly sent to Paraguay in 1956 as "technical advisors" to the Paraguayan police.
The police's Technical Affairs Directorate, right in the heart of the capital Asuncion, became one of the most feared clandestine torture centres of the Stroessner regime.
The compensation request will be sent to President Bill Clinton and to the Human Rights Committee of the U.S. Senate.

Barreto said the aim was "to begin legal proceedings to get compensation from the United States of $4.4 million (corrects from $.4 billion) for more than 400 prisoners of conscience, who spent a total of 1,209 days in jail."
The former detainee said the request was to have been taken to Washington by Paraguayan Senate President Miguel Saguier, now on a visit to the United States.
"But a lot of people still think Paraguay is a North American protectorate and it seems Saguier did not want to upset his hosts, so he forgot the letter," said Barreto.
